extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and principal investigators preparing NIH grant applications (R01/R25) / grant writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and critique on writing NIH grant applications (examples drawn from NIAID sample R01s and an R25 FOA), focusing on Specific Aims, Innovation, measurable impact for education/outreach, and FOA compliance. Useful for PIs preparing competing continuations or new R01/R25 submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Aims clarity and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific Aims should be concrete and not framed with vague, exploratory verbs (example criticized: 'Dissect the mechanism...', 'Understand the function...', 'Discover a comprehensive set of apicoplast proteins...'). The post labels overbroad aims as a 'Fishing Expedition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague aims like 'understand' or 'discover a comprehensive set' that suggest unfocused, exploratory work. State precise, testable objectives and avoid language that reads as a broad fishing expedition. Give specific, bounded goals that reviewers can judge for feasibility and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation section must be concrete and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: The Innovation section should not consist of generic claims or passive statements such as 'We would like to argue that our project has been highly innovative...'—the blog criticizes passive voice and lack of concrete points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly describe the novel technological aspects and biological insights, with concrete examples of what is new about the approach, concepts, or hypotheses. Don't rely on assertions of innovation; show it with specifics the reviewer can latch onto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice and generic puffery
rubrics_metrics.description: The post calls out passive constructions ('We would like to argue', 'We feel that overall this investment has paid off') and generic, non-specific language as an anti-pattern in grant prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write actively and precisely. Replace passive/generic phrases with direct statements about what will be tested, how it is different, and why it matters. Passive/generic statements obscure significance and innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight technological aspects and biological insights
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers noted that 'The technological aspects and biological insights that are innovative could have been better highlighted by the investigator.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming innovation, map it to concrete technologies, methods, or biological discoveries. Explain how these will change understanding or enable new experiments; link innovations to aims and expected outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat only high-scoring sample grants as universal templates
rubrics_metrics.description: The author warns that posting only sample grants that scored in the 2-7%ile range gives newcomers an inaccurate view; excellent grants can hide problems and are not the only model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a range of sample applications (including near-misses) to learn where grants fail or succeed. Be skeptical of treating funded applications as perfect templates—they may benefit from context (prior productivity, reputation) that won't apply to all applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of 'grantsmithing' vs. fundability
rubrics_metrics.description: The post argues that the grantsmithing differences between, e.g., a 4%ile and a 14%ile grant may be irrelevant to ultimate fundability; other factors (productivity, program-level support) can dominate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume polishing prose alone will secure funding. Address substantive issues reviewers care about (data, feasibility, prior productivity, fit to IC priorities) in addition to presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: For R25 FOAs: require outreach to large audience with measurable success
rubrics_metrics.description: PAR-11-086 (NIAID Science Education Awards R25) expects education programs to 'provide outreach to a large audience of students at a national level... using approaches where successes can be measured.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design education/outreach projects with clear, measurable outcomes and evaluation plans. Define target audience scale and metrics for success up front; reviewers expect measurable impact, not just dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and describe measurable impact assessment methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes that measuring the 'success' of scientific blogging or internet-based outreach is not easy but that 'there already exist ways to try to measure impact' (e.g., polls, short evaluations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete assessment tools (analytics, surveys, evaluation instruments) in the application. Provide plausible plans for data collection and metrics (pre/post tests, usage stats, survey instruments, etc.) and cite prior experience if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available web/survey tools to collect impact data
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical suggestion: brief post-seminar evaluation surveys can be done with SurveyMonkey, PollDaddy, or web polls; NIH websites sometimes use polls to monitor impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement simple, validated survey instruments and web analytics to demonstrate reach and effect. Describe frequency, sample sizes, and analysis approaches so reviewers see the plan is credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check FOA-specific receipt dates and IC-specific policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The post advises that some NIH ICs use nonstandard or once-per-year receipt dates for certain mechanisms; applicants should check their IC's announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before preparing an application, verify the FOA's receipt dates, IC-specific application instructions, and any special review/administrative policies. Missing or mis-timed submissions risk automatic noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to FOA budget and duration limits
rubrics_metrics.description: For the cited R25 FOA: 'You may request up to $175,000 per year in direct costs and propose up to 5 years of support.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure budgets and timelines to fit the FOA limits. If you need exceptions or subawards that change direct costs, follow FOA instructions and explain justification clearly to avoid administrative triage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use NIH RePORTER to identify currently funded projects under the mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion: 'Start with RePORTER to see what is currently funded by the NIH under the R25 mechanism (New Grants, Existing Grants).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey RePORTER results to learn what types of projects get funded, common budgets and scopes, and potential gaps your project could fill. Cite similar funded projects when appropriate to argue feasibility and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of project-based vs. program-based framing
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a tension between the NIH's formal project-based funding approach and investigators' de facto program-based research; prior productivity can make reviewers 'like the research program.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame competing continuations or long-term labs carefully: if applying as a project, focus aims and innovation on the specific project; if success depends on a broader program, document prior productivity and how the program-level resources will enable proposed aims.
